issues: Numbers reproduce exactly on re-run (control 0.16%, full sweep identical to result.json) and model.py self-test passes all 4 controls. The control (spread_mult=0.01 vs deterministic) is NON-vacuous: stochastic=False feeds 3 IDENTICAL scenarios (half=0) while spread_mult=0.01 feeds 3 near-identical-but-distinct scenarios, so the 0.16% gap is genuine convergence, not a tautology. The flagged failure classes are absent: not pure-CVaR (cvar=None here), the baseline does not secretly equal a stochastic path, and the monotonicity is BOUNDED not runaway -- I swept spread_mult to 0.25/3/5/10/20 and cost saturates at mean=1.7165/p95=3.0003 by ~sm=3 because p10=max(0,mu-dev) clips the low scenario at PV=0; widening further is a no-op. 'Wider bands are better here' is explainable (more conservative pre-hedging pays off against the aft_sd=0.3 truth distribution) and self-limiting. ONE FACTUAL ERROR in the prior agent's takeaways: takeaway #1 claims the worst mis-sizing (0.5x) is '8.2% below the deterministic baseline mean'. Actual rel-vs-det: 0.5x = -5.01%, and -8.10% is the NOMINAL 1.0x case. The author conflated the two. Qualitative claim (all spread_mults beat deterministic) survives -- 0.5x is still 5% below det -- but the magnitude is wrong and the real story is that mis-sizing to 0.5x erodes ~38% of the Phase 2 advantage (8.1pp -> 5.0pp), which is more than the '8.2%, barely dented' framing implies. The 0.75->1.0 p95 near-tie (+0.39%) is within the disclosed ~+/-10% p95 sampling variance. Caveats are honest and adequate.
final_takeaways: Phase 2 (stochastic) beats the deterministic baseline at every spread_mult tested, but the advantage is calibration-sensitive: nominal (1.0x) is -8.1% vs deterministic, while the worst under-sizing (0.5x, too-narrow bands) is only -5.0% vs deterministic. So mis-sizing to half-width erodes roughly 38% of the Phase 2 edge -- it does not destroy the advantage, but it materially dents it. (NOTE: the prior agent's '8.2% below deterministic' for 0.5x is wrong; -8.1% is the 1.0x case, 0.5x is -5.0%.)

Cost is monotone-decreasing in spread_mult over the tested 0.5-2.0 range but this is NOT pathological: it saturates by ~spread_mult=3 (mean plateaus at 1.7165, p95 at 3.0003) because the low scenario p10=max(0, mu-dev) floors at zero PV, after which wider bands are a no-op. The 'wider is better' direction reflects that conservative pre-hedging pays off against this aft_sd=0.3 truth distribution, and it is self-limiting -- there is no runaway over-hedge.

Direction of error matters: narrowing bands (spread_mult<1) is the costly mistake (mean +3.4%, p95 +10.5% vs nominal at 0.5x), while over-dispersing (spread_mult>1) is cheap and slightly beneficial (mean -1.6 to -1.8%, p95 -2.3 to -6.4%). When uncertain how to calibrate, err wide, not narrow.

The p95 tail is more sensitive to under-sizing than the mean (+10.5% vs +3.4% at 0.5x), so data-driven calibration matters most for tail-risk control. But with only 80 days (~4-5 days in the p95 tail) the p95 estimates carry ~+/-10% sampling variance -- the 0.75-vs-1.0 p95 near-tie (+0.39%) is within noise and should not be read as a real inversion.

The control (spread_mult=0.01 -> within 0.16% of deterministic, threshold 5%) is a valid, non-vacuous self-consistency check: the near-zero-spread stochastic LP correctly degenerates toward the P50 controller without exactly reproducing it, confirming the spread_mult mechanism and the two-stage LP formulation are sound.
